The carboxyl group is also less susceptible to nucleophilic attack than aldehydes and ketones, because the carbon atom of the carboxyl group is less electrophilic, due to delocalization of one of lone-pair of hydroxyl group with carbonyl (Section 20.2).

Similarly the carbonyl group withdraws electrons from hydroxyl, making the O–H bond more polar and it becomes easier for the hydrogen atom to ionize than O–H bond of alcohols. Hence, carboxylic acids are more acidic than alcohols.

20.7 Reactions of Carboxylic Acids

Following are some of the reactions of carboxylic acids that involve the conversion of the carboxylic acids to their derivatives as well as synthesis of some other compounds.

20.7.1 Conversion to Carboxylic Acid Derivatives

20.7.1.1 Conversion to Acyl Halides

Acyl halides or acid halides are the most reactive of carboxylic acid derivatives and they can be used for preparation of other functional derivatives of carboxylic acid. Acyl chlorides are more common and less expensive than bromides and iodides. They are usually prepared by replacing the –OH of carboxyl with –Cl, using thionyl chloride or phosphorous pentachloride.

20.7.1.2 Conversion to Acid Anhydrides

Acid anhydrides are derived from acids by removing water from two carboxylic acid molecules. As the name indicates, these are anhydrous carboxylic acids. They are actually diacyl oxides. The dehydration of water from carboxylic acid to form anhydride, can be accomplished by using dehydration agents like phosphorous pentaoxide.

20.7.1.3 Conversion to Esters

Esters are a class of organic compounds that are derived from acids by replacing the hydroxyl group (–OH) by an alkoxy group (–OR). They are obtained by elimination of water molecule from an acid and an alcohol.

When a carboxylic acid and an alcohol are heated in the presence of an acid catalyst, an equilibrium is established with the formation of ester and water. This reaction is reversible and called esterification (Section 18.1.7.4). The position of equilibrium can be made more favorable in the right, by using either the alcohol or the carboxylic acid in excess, or removing water from the reaction mixture.

Ethyl acetate is an important ester which can be prepared by this method by the reaction of acetic acid with ethanol.

Esters can also be prepared by the reaction of an alcohol with acid halide or acid anhydride (alcoholysis of acid halide or anhydride). In case of conversion of acid halide to ester, pyridine base is used to consume the HCl formed in reaction.

The carboxyl group is also less susceptible to nucleophilic attack than aldehydes and ketones, because the carbon atom of the carboxyl group is less electrophilic, due to delocalization of one of lone-pair of hydroxyl group with carbonyl (Section 20.2).

Similarly the carbonyl group withdraws electrons from hydroxyl, making the O–H bond more polar and it becomes easier for the hydrogen atom to ionize than O–H bond of alcohols. Hence, carboxylic acids are more acidic than alcohols.

20.7 Reactions of Carboxylic Acids

Following are some of the reactions of carboxylic acids that involve the conversion of the carboxylic acids to their derivatives as well as synthesis of some other compounds.

20.7.1 Conversion to Carboxylic Acid Derivatives

20.7.1.1 Conversion to Acyl Halides

Acyl halides or acid halides are the most reactive of carboxylic acid derivatives and they can be used for preparation of other functional derivatives of carboxylic acid. Acyl chlorides are more common and less expensive than bromides and iodides. They are usually prepared by replacing the –OH of carboxyl with –Cl, using thionyl chloride or phosphorous pentachloride.

20.7.1.2 Conversion to Acid Anhydrides

Acid anhydrides are derived from acids by removing water from two carboxylic acid molecules. As the name indicates, these are anhydrous carboxylic acids. They are actually diacyl oxides. The dehydration of water from carboxylic acid to form anhydride, can be accomplished by using dehydration agents like phosphorous pentaoxide.

20.7.1.3 Conversion to Esters

Esters are a class of organic compounds that are derived from acids by replacing the hydroxyl group (–OH) by an alkoxy group (–OR). They are obtained by elimination of water molecule from an acid and an alcohol.

When a carboxylic acid and an alcohol are heated in the presence of an acid catalyst, an equilibrium is established with the formation of ester and water. This reaction is reversible and called esterification (Section 18.1.7.4). The position of equilibrium can be made more favorable in the right, by using either the alcohol or the carboxylic acid in excess, or removing water from the reaction mixture.

Ethyl acetate is an important ester which can be prepared by this method by the reaction of acetic acid with ethanol.

Esters can also be prepared by the reaction of an alcohol with acid halide or acid anhydride (alcoholysis of acid halide or anhydride). In case of conversion of acid halide to ester, pyridine base is used to consume the HCl formed in reaction.
